No answer leak detected. The problem is a classical result following from Montel's theorem. Here is the proof.

---

**Theorem.** Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}$ be open and let $\{f_n\}$ be a sequence of holomorphic functions on $\Omega$ that is uniformly bounded (i.e., $|f_n(z)| \le M$ for all $z \in \Omega$ and all $n$) and converges pointwise on $\Omega$ to a function $f$. Then $f_n \to f$ uniformly on every compact subset of $\Omega$. In particular, $f$ is holomorphic.

**Proof.**

Since $|f_n(z)| \le M$ for all $n$ and all $z \in \Omega$, the family $\{f_n\}$ is uniformly bounded on $\Omega$, hence locally uniformly bounded. By **Montel's theorem**, $\{f_n\}$ is a **normal family**: every subsequence of $\{f_n\}$ admits a further subsequence that converges uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$ to a holomorphic function.

The pointwise limit $f$ satisfies $|f(z)| \le M$ for all $z \in \Omega$, since $|f(z)| = \lim |f_n(z)| \le M$.

Let $K \subset \Omega$ be compact. We show $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $K$.

Suppose for contradiction that the convergence is not uniform on $K$. Then there exists $\varepsilon > 0$, a subsequence $\{f_{n_j}\}$, and points $z_j \in K$ such that
$$|f_{n_j}(z_j) - f(z_j)| \ge \varepsilon \quad \text{for all } j.$$

By Montel's theorem, the subsequence $\{f_{n_j}\}$ has a further subsequence $\{f_{n_{j_k}}\}$ that converges uniformly on compact subsets of $\Omega$ to a holomorphic function $g$. Uniform convergence on compact sets implies pointwise convergence, so $g(z) = \lim_{k\to\infty} f_{n_{j_k}}(z)$ for every $z \in \Omega$. But $\{f_{n_{j_k}}\}$ is also a subsequence of the original pointwise-convergent sequence $\{f_n\}$, so $f_{n_{j_k}}(z) \to f(z)$ pointwise. By uniqueness of pointwise limits, $g = f$ on $\Omega$.

Therefore $f_{n_{j_k}} \to f$ uniformly on $K$:
$$\sup_{z \in K} |f_{n_{j_k}}(z) - f(z)| \xrightarrow{k \to \infty} 0.$$

Since $z_{j_k} \in K$, we have
$$|f_{n_{j_k}}(z_{j_k}) - f(z_{j_k})| \le \sup_{z \in K} |f_{n_{j_k}}(z) - f(z)| \to 0,$$
contradicting $|f_{n_{j_k}}(z_{j_k}) - f(z_{j_k})| \ge \varepsilon$ for all $k$.

This contradiction establishes that $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $K$. Since $K$ was an arbitrary compact subset of $\Omega$, the convergence is uniform on every compact subset of $\Omega$.

Finally, since each $f_n$ is holomorphic and $f_n \to f$ uniformly on compact sets, a standard consequence of Morera's theorem (or Weierstrass's theorem on uniformly convergent sequences of holomorphic functions) shows that $f$ is holomorphic on $\Omega$. $\blacksquare$

---

**Remark.** This is a special case of **Vitali's convergence theorem**, which requires only local uniform boundedness and pointwise convergence on a set with an accumulation point in $\Omega$. The hypotheses here (global uniform boundedness and pointwise convergence on all of $\Omega$) are strictly stronger, so the conclusion follows a fortiori.

### PROOF COMPLETE
